title: The word — a myth, a tribunal and a tape measure
learning_goal: Know where 'bespoke' really comes from, that the Row's origin story is false, that a 2008 ruling took the word away, and that the answer was the 100-yard rule.

narration.script: Where does the word bespoke come from? The word is about fifty years older than the first tailor on this street. The trade tells it differently: cloth spoken for by a customer, right here. The dates say no. In June two thousand and eight the Row took a cheaper rival to the advertising regulator: four-hundred-and-ninety-five-pound suits, machine-sewn abroad, sold as bespoke. The Row lost. Bespoke and made-to-measure, the regulator said, now mean much the same thing. The other pressure is rent. A chain store opened at number three in 2013; in 2016 the council wrote planning protection for tailoring on this street. So they stopped defending the word and defined the thing — by geography: made within a hundred yards of Savile Row. A hundred and sixty-nine firms in 1912. Nineteen by 2006. Twenty-two houses today — and the Row's first woman head cutter in 2009, with her own shop by 2016.
